title: Tai Chi for Arthritis: Evidence and Getting Started
meta_title: Tai Chi for Arthritis: Evidence and UK Class Checklist
meta_description: What tai chi research shows for osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, plus UK class questions, adaptations and when to get medical advice.
excerpt: What tai chi research shows for osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, plus UK class questions, adaptations and when to get medical advice.
direct_answer: Tai chi may help some people with knee osteoarthritis, but rheumatoid arthritis evidence is uncertain. Choose an adapted class, ask about the teacher's experience and follow your own exercise restrictions. It is not a cure or a replacement for medicines, physiotherapy or assessment of new joint symptoms.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: tai chi arthritis UK, tai chi joint pain, tai chi beginners arthritis, tai chi balance, tai chi classes UK
content:
Tai chi combines slow movements, attention and controlled breathing. It is one way to be active, rather than a cure for arthritis or a replacement for treatment. Some people enjoy its pace and group setting; others prefer walking, water-based activity or a different exercise programme.

The useful question is not whether tai chi is the best exercise for everyone. It is whether an adapted class fits your condition, balance, goals and preferences. This guide explains the evidence and gives questions to ask before starting. It does not prescribe a movement sequence or replace an individual physiotherapy plan.

Does tai chi help osteoarthritis?

Research suggests that tai chi can help some people with knee osteoarthritis manage symptoms and everyday movement. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health evidence summary describes encouraging findings, but also differences between studies and uncertainty about the best style, frequency and duration.

A 2016 randomised trial compared tai chi with a course of physiotherapy in 204 people with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis. Both groups improved in pain and function, with benefits followed for up to 52 weeks. Participants knew which treatment they received, and the researchers noted uncertainty about applying the findings to other settings.

That is evidence about particular programmes for knee osteoarthritis. It does not show that any online video equals personalised physiotherapy, that tai chi repairs cartilage, or that everyone will improve by a set percentage. A class cannot assess every cause of new pain or replace rehabilitation after surgery.

Is the evidence the same for rheumatoid arthritis?

No. The 2019 Cochrane review of seven studies involving 345 people concerned rheumatoid arthritis, not knee or hip osteoarthritis. The evidence for pain, function and disease activity was very uncertain. It should not be described as proof that tai chi treats rheumatoid inflammation.

A 2023 review also found limited, uncertain evidence, with small studies and risk of bias. You may still find an adapted activity enjoyable, but enjoyment is different from evidence that it controls disease. Keep taking prescribed medicines as instructed and discuss concerns with your rheumatology team. Do not reduce disease-controlling treatment because a class feels helpful.

Does NICE specifically recommend tai chi?

NICE guidance for osteoarthritis recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to the person's needs, such as local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness. It also says to consider supervised exercise. Those recommendations are not a blanket endorsement of every tai chi programme, instructor or commercial course.

The NIH summary describes a tai chi recommendation from US professional bodies for knee and hip osteoarthritis. That is a different guideline, not an NHS or NICE endorsement. You do not need an endorsement claim to ask whether a particular class could fit your exercise plan.

Who should ask for individual advice before a class?

Ask your physiotherapist or healthcare team about suitability if you have falls, poor balance, a recent operation, marked joint instability or symptoms that make standing and turning difficult. Follow your own postoperative restrictions rather than a class's standard instructions. If you have been inactive or have other health conditions, explain this when discussing a starting level.

Slow movement can still challenge balance and load a painful joint. A seated option may be useful, but it is not automatically suitable for everyone. Ask how the teacher adapts weight shifts, turns and knee bending, and whether you can remain seated or stop without pressure to keep up. Do not practise an unsupported standing sequence to test whether you are safe enough for it.

How can you find a suitable UK class?

The Tai Chi Union instructor directory is one place to look for local or online teaching. It includes different internal arts and classes with different aims, including martial arts. A listing is a starting point for questions, not proof of arthritis expertise or medical suitability. The directory states that it does not carry out background checks on instructors.

You can also ask a local leisure or community centre what it currently offers. Check availability, access and charges directly rather than relying on an old price or timetable. Before committing, ask:

  • Is this a beginners' health-focused class, and what experience do you have adapting it for arthritis?
  • Can I observe or try a session before paying for a course?
  • Are seated versions, rest breaks and shorter participation possible?
  • Are the entrance, toilets and practice space accessible for my needs?
  • What happens if a movement causes pain, dizziness or loss of balance?
  • What are the full fees and cancellation terms?

Tell the teacher about relevant limitations and your clinician's restrictions. You do not have to share more personal medical detail with a group than you are comfortable sharing.

What should you check before practising at home?

Ask the instructor which movements you can repeat safely and which to leave until they can observe you. An online teacher may not see your whole body or notice a balance problem. Check whether the session is live or recorded and whether individual feedback is available.

Clear enough space to move without catching your feet or bumping furniture. If you have been advised to practise seated, the NHS sitting-exercise guidance advises a solid, stable chair without wheels, with feet flat on the floor. Do not assume a light chair or movable table is a safe support for standing work. Ask for an assessed setup if you need support to stand.

Begin with an amount agreed for your situation, not the length of a research session or an entire video. You can watch part of a lesson without copying it. A shorter, manageable practice is more useful than forcing yourself to finish movements you cannot control.

How should you judge progress without a promised deadline?

Choose an everyday goal, such as feeling more confident with a familiar movement or finding an activity you enjoy repeating. Note what you did and how you felt during and afterwards. Discuss persistent worsening or repeated difficulty with your teacher and healthcare team rather than adding more practice automatically.

There is no reliable promise that benefits start after six or eight weeks for every person. Research programmes vary and their results are group averages. Tai chi may form one part of a wider exercise plan; ask whether you also need strength, aerobic or balance work suited to your needs. Do not interpret a calmer session as evidence that joint inflammation has gone away.

When should you stop and get medical advice?

For osteoarthritis, NICE explains that some pain or discomfort can occur when starting therapeutic exercise. This is not an instruction to push through every symptom. The NHS rheumatoid arthritis guide advises stopping and resting if an activity causes severe pain or makes joints warm and swollen. Seek individual advice if this keeps happening.

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for sudden severe joint pain, new swelling or a hot or discoloured joint, especially if you feel unwell, hot, cold or shivery. Septic arthritis needs prompt assessment and can occur without a fever. Do not try to exercise a newly swollen joint until it loosens up.

What is a useful first step?

Write down your main limitation, any exercise restrictions and one question for a prospective teacher. Ask about adaptations and access before booking. If suitability is uncertain, take those details to your physiotherapist. You can decide that tai chi is not for you and choose another activity without having failed an arthritis treatment.
